question: Why did net sales change between August and September 2026?

report.summary: Net sales fell by 8,500 cents from August to September 2026. The data show gross sales rose by 10,000 cents, but refunds rose by 18,500 cents; most of the refund increase came from the small-customer segment. The records show amounts and dates, not why refunds were requested, so they cannot establish the reasons behind the change.

findings.statement: Overall net sales were 191,500 cents in August and 183,000 cents in September, a decline of 8,500 cents. Overall gross sales increased from 194,000 cents to 204,000 cents, while refunds increased from 2,500 cents to 21,000 cents.

The small segment's net sales dropped from 56,500 cents to 49,000 cents, while its refunds rose from 2,500 cents to 16,000 cents. The large segment's net sales changed from 135,000 cents to 134,000 cents, with refunds rising from zero to 5,000 cents.

The net-sales decline is explained arithmetically by refunds increasing more than gross sales: gross sales rose by 10,000 cents, but refunds rose by 18,500 cents. Segment results indicate the larger part of the refund increase was in small customers (13,500 cents), versus 5,000 cents in large customers.
The data cannot establish why customers requested refunds; they contain refund amounts and dates but not refund reasons.

assumptions: Periods are August 1 through September 1, 2026 (August) and September 1 through October 1, 2026 (September), using UTC half-open date ranges.
Amounts are integer USD cents. Gross sales use order dates; refunds use refund dates and are attributed to the segment of the customer on the original order.
Segment totals were checked against overall totals and reconcile for both months.
open_questions: What reasons were recorded for refunds in each month and customer segment?
Would checking order-level refund counts and refund timing clarify what drove September's increase?

queries.purpose: Compare gross sales, refunds, and net sales across August and September 2026
queries.sql: WITH month_keys AS (SELECT '2026-08-01' AS start_date, '2026-09-01' AS end_date UNION ALL SELECT '2026-09-01', '2026-10-01'), gross_by_month AS (SELECT m.start_date, m.end_date, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount_cents),0) AS gross FROM month_keys m LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_date >= m.start_date AND o.order_date < m.end_date GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date), refunds_by_month AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,COALESCE(SUM(r.amount_cents),0) AS refunds FROM month_keys m LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.refund_date >= m.start_date AND r.refund_date < m.end_date GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date) SELECT g.start_date,g.end_date,g.gross, r.refunds, g.gross-r.refunds AS net FROM gross_by_month g JOIN refunds_by_month r USING(start_date,end_date) ORDER BY g.start_date

queries.purpose: Break down monthly gross sales and refunds by customer segment to see which segments drove the changes
queries.sql: WITH month_keys AS (SELECT '2026-08-01' AS start_date,'2026-09-01' AS end_date UNION ALL SELECT '2026-09-01','2026-10-01'), gross_segment AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,c.segment,SUM(o.amount_cents) AS gross FROM month_keys m JOIN orders o ON o.order_date >= m.start_date AND o.order_date < m.end_date JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id=o.customer_id GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date,c.segment), refund_segment AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,c.segment,SUM(r.amount_cents) AS refunds FROM month_keys m JOIN refunds r ON r.refund_date >= m.start_date AND r.refund_date < m.end_date JOIN orders o ON o.order_id=r.order_id JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id=o.customer_id GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date,c.segment), segments AS (SELECT start_date,end_date,segment FROM gross_segment UNION SELECT start_date,end_date,segment FROM refund_segment) SELECT s.start_date,s.end_date,s.segment,COALESCE(g.gross,0) AS gross,COALESCE(r.refunds,0) AS refunds,COALESCE(g.gross,0)-COALESCE(r.refunds,0) AS net FROM segments s LEFT JOIN gross_segment g USING(start_date,end_date,segment) LEFT JOIN refund_segment r USING(start_date,end_date,segment) ORDER BY s.start_date,s.segment

queries.purpose: Verify that segment totals reconcile to monthly overall gross sales, refunds, and net sales
queries.sql: WITH month_keys AS (SELECT '2026-08-01' AS start_date,'2026-09-01' AS end_date UNION ALL SELECT '2026-09-01','2026-10-01'), gross_by_month AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,COALESCE(SUM(o.amount_cents),0) AS gross FROM month_keys m LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_date>=m.start_date AND o.order_date<m.end_date GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date), refund_by_month AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,COALESCE(SUM(r.amount_cents),0) AS refunds FROM month_keys m LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.refund_date>=m.start_date AND r.refund_date<m.end_date GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date), segment_gross AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,c.segment,SUM(o.amount_cents) AS gross FROM month_keys m JOIN orders o ON o.order_date>=m.start_date AND o.order_date<m.end_date JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id=o.customer_id GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date,c.segment), segment_refunds AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,c.segment,SUM(r.amount_cents) AS refunds FROM month_keys m JOIN refunds r ON r.refund_date>=m.start_date AND r.refund_date<m.end_date JOIN orders o ON o.order_id=r.order_id JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id=o.customer_id GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date,c.segment), segment_totals AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,COALESCE(SUM(sg.gross),0) AS gross,COALESCE(SUM(sr.refunds),0) AS refunds FROM month_keys m LEFT JOIN segment_gross sg USING(start_date,end_date) LEFT JOIN segment_refunds sr USING(start_date,end_date) GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date) SELECT g.start_date,g.end_date,g.gross AS overall_gross,s.gross AS segment_gross_sum,g.refunds AS overall_refunds,s.refunds AS segment_refund_sum,g.gross-g.refunds AS overall_net,s.gross-s.refunds AS segment_net_sum FROM gross_by_month g JOIN refund_by_month r USING(start_date,end_date) JOIN segment_totals s USING(start_date,end_date) ORDER BY g.start_date

messages.content:
You investigate questions about a fictional company's sales with read-only SQL over a small SQLite database.

## How to work

1. Call `run_sql` for a first look. Compute every figure in SQL, not in your head.
2. Read the result, then choose at least one follow-up query based on it, for example separating gross sales from refunds or comparing customer segments.
3. You have at most 6 query attempts, and errors count. Two to four queries are usually enough.
4. Call `submit_report` once the results answer the question.

## Metric rules in SQL

- Apply the business rules below even where they differ from the usual meaning of a metric name.
- Use half-open periods: `order_date >= '2026-08-01' AND order_date < '2026-09-01'`. Filter refunds by `refund_date`, never by the date of their order.
- Aggregate orders and refunds in separate subqueries, then combine them. Joining refund rows to orders repeats order amounts.
- Join only on keys: `refunds.order_id = orders.order_id` and `orders.customer_id = customers.customer_id`. A refund's segment is the segment of the customer on its original order.
- Keep each query to one breakdown, and give CTEs names that differ from the table names.
- Before you report a breakdown, check that its parts add up to the overall totals. If they do not, fix the query.

## Report

- Every figure in `metrics` must appear exactly as a cell in the result of the query it cites, for example `q2`. Query any total or segment figure you need.
- Attach every amount you mention to a finding's `metrics`. A change between periods is the one exception: attach the figure for each period and write only the difference in the text.
- In text, write money only as an integer followed by "cents", for example "183000 cents". Do not use "$" or dollars; the application formats money.
- `observed`: shown directly by a query result. `inferred`: a conclusion drawn from observed figures. `unknown`: something the question asks about that the data cannot establish.
- Refund rows record amounts and dates, not why customers asked for refunds. When the question asks why, add an `unknown` finding for the part the data cannot explain, such as the reasons for refunds, instead of guessing. Use `open_questions` for checks that could narrow it down.
- State the periods, units and any other assumption. If the question does not name periods, choose them from the data and say so.

# Business data investigation: exercise rules

These fictional rules are the source of truth for this assignment. No industry research is required.

1. Use customers, orders, and refunds. IDs link refunds to orders and orders to customers; one order can have multiple refunds.
2. Gross sales for a period sum orders by order_date. Refunds for that period sum refunds by refund_date. Net sales equal gross sales minus refunds. Use UTC dates and half-open periods: start included, end excluded.
3. Use integer USD cents. Group order and refund totals separately before combining them; joining raw refund rows to orders can repeat order amounts.
4. Assign refunds to the segment of the customer on the original order. The records show amounts and dates, not why a customer requested a refund.

## Schema

```sql
CREATE TABLE customers (customer_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, segment TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE orders (order_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id), order_date TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(amount_cents >= 0));
CREATE TABLE refunds (refund_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, order_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(order_id), refund_date TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(amount_cents >= 0));
```
Why did net sales change between August and September 2026?

function.arguments: {"purpose":"Verify that segment totals reconcile to monthly overall gross sales, refunds, and net sales","sql":"WITH month_keys AS (SELECT '2026-08-01' AS start_date,'2026-09-01' AS end_date UNION ALL SELECT '2026-09-01','2026-10-01'), gross_by_month AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,COALESCE(SUM(o.amount_cents),0) AS gross FROM month_keys m LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_date>=m.start_date AND o.order_date<m.end_date GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date), refund_by_month AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,COALESCE(SUM(r.amount_cents),0) AS refunds FROM month_keys m LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.refund_date>=m.start_date AND r.refund_date<m.end_date GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date), segment_gross AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,c.segment,SUM(o.amount_cents) AS gross FROM month_keys m JOIN orders o ON o.order_date>=m.start_date AND o.order_date<m.end_date JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id=o.customer_id GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date,c.segment), segment_refunds AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,c.segment,SUM(r.amount_cents) AS refunds FROM month_keys m JOIN refunds r ON r.refund_date>=m.start_date AND r.refund_date<m.end_date JOIN orders o ON o.order_id=r.order_id JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id=o.customer_id GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date,c.segment), segment_totals AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,COALESCE(SUM(sg.gross),0) AS gross,COALESCE(SUM(sr.refunds),0) AS refunds FROM month_keys m LEFT JOIN segment_gross sg USING(start_date,end_date) LEFT JOIN segment_refunds sr USING(start_date,end_date) GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date) SELECT g.start_date,g.end_date,g.gross AS overall_gross,s.gross AS segment_gross_sum,g.refunds AS overall_refunds,s.refunds AS segment_refund_sum,g.gross-g.refunds AS overall_net,s.gross-s.refunds AS segment_net_sum FROM gross_by_month g JOIN refund_by_month r USING(start_date,end_date) JOIN segment_totals s USING(start_date,end_date) ORDER BY g.start_date"}
function.name: run_sql

function.arguments: {"purpose":"Reconcile overall monthly totals against customer-segment sums","sql":"WITH month_keys AS (SELECT '2026-08-01' AS start_date,'2026-09-01' AS end_date UNION ALL SELECT '2026-09-01','2026-10-01'), gross_month AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,COALESCE(SUM(o.amount_cents),0) AS gross FROM month_keys m LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_date>=m.start_date AND o.order_date<m.end_date GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date), refund_month AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,COALESCE(SUM(r.amount_cents),0) AS refunds FROM month_keys m LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.refund_date>=m.start_date AND r.refund_date<m.end_date GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date), gross_segment AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,c.segment,SUM(o.amount_cents) AS gross FROM month_keys m JOIN orders o ON o.order_date>=m.start_date AND o.order_date<m.end_date JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id=o.customer_id GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date,c.segment), refund_segment AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,c.segment,SUM(r.amount_cents) AS refunds FROM month_keys m JOIN refunds r ON r.refund_date>=m.start_date AND r.refund_date<m.end_date JOIN orders o ON o.order_id=r.order_id JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id=o.customer_id GROUP BY m.start_date,m.end_date,c.segment), segment_sums AS (SELECT m.start_date,m.end_date,COALESCE((SELECT SUM(gross) FROM gross_segment x WHERE x.start_date=m.start_date),0) AS gross,COALESCE((SELECT SUM(refunds) FROM refund_segment x WHERE x.start_date=m.start_date),0) AS refunds FROM month_keys m) SELECT g.start_date,g.end_date,g.gross AS overall_gross,s.gross AS segment_gross_sum,r.refunds AS overall_refunds,s.refunds AS segment_refund_sum,g.gross-r.refunds AS overall_net,s.gross-s.refunds AS segment_net_sum FROM gross_month g JOIN refund_month r USING(start_date,end_date) JOIN segment_sums s USING(start_date,end_date) ORDER BY g.start_date"}
function.name: run_sql
